1:
Ellicott sets the chapter in its place. The table of nations has just carried the reader over the whole known world, from Armenia and the rivers to the Nile valley, Palestine and the islands, with Lud moving into Asia Minor and the sons of Japheth breaking into Europe between the Caspian and the Black Sea; now the narrative doubles back to give the reason for that dispersion. He renders the opening phrase literally as of one lip and of words one, meaning that pronunciation and vocabulary alike were the same, and adds a note of his own time, that where the gulf between Sanscrit and the Semitic tongues was lately thought unbridgeable, recent inquiry tends to show a common basis under both. Clarke has no doubt which language it was, taking it for Hebrew and resting the claim on the proper names of Scripture; he passes on the reckoning that the tongue served all the world until Peleg was born, and the Hebrews alone thereafter until the captivity, when it went out of common use.

Gill reports the Targum's version, that the generations of the earth were of one language and one counsel, speaking the holy tongue in which the world was created, and takes exception to the middle term. The one language he grants; the one counsel he does not, since it does not appear all were of a mind about the city and the tower, and he thinks it unlikely Shem and his sons were in the design. Henry sets the scene before the building begins. After the flood the families had been assigned their several ways, either by Noah's appointment or by agreement among his sons; but men were loth to disperse, reckoning the more the merrier and the safer, and were slack to go and possess the land God had given them, thinking themselves wiser than either God or Noah. Two things, he says, befriended their design. One was the common language, since while they understood one another they would be the likelier to love one another and the abler to help one another, and the less inclined to part — a point Wesley repeats. The other was the plain, spacious enough to hold them and fruitful enough to keep them, though they never asked what room there would be once their numbers grew; and Henry draws the moral that present conveniences often tempt men to neglect both duty and interest for the future.

Why they built at all is where Calvin parts company with the others. Some had supposed the tower a refuge against a second flood; Calvin says those who conjecture this have no guide but the dream of their own brain, since the words note nothing but mad ambition and proud contempt of God. Henry, who reports the same guess, meets it with a practical objection: men with that in view would have built on a mountain, not a plain. What Calvin finds in the text is the wish for a name. To erect a citadel was no great crime, but to raise a monument that should endure through all ages was headstrong pride, and he hears behind it the fable of the giants heaping mountains on mountains to pull Jove from his throne, since men inflated beyond measure make war on God whether they profess it or not. On the date he weighs a fragment allowing a hundred and thirty years from the flood against the Jewish reckoning of about three hundred and forty, and thinks Moses settles it, since Peleg, in whose days the earth was divided, stands only a century down the line. He closes on Noah, who must have been wounded to the depth by such a counsel among his own posterity, and takes it as God exercising the holy man in extreme old age, to teach us not to be discouraged by a continual succession of conflicts.
2:
Which way they travelled is disputed on the first phrase. Gill notes that some would render it not from the east but eastward, since Ararat lay north of Shinar and men coming from there might rather be said to come from the north. Ellicott presses that reading and admits what it costs, since all the versions have from the east; but Ararat is north-west of Shinar and no part of Armenia can be called east of Babylonia, and though the Chaldean legends put the ark on a mountain east of Assyria, he cannot explain how the name would then have travelled to Armenia, which the Bible elsewhere seems to make the cradle of the race. Most modern commentators therefore read eastward, as the word plainly means two chapters later. Clarke defends the received rendering by usage, since Assyria and Mesopotamia and the country beyond the Euphrates are called the east throughout Scripture — Balaam is fetched from the mountains of the east though he lived on the Euphrates, the wise men come from the east, Abraham is said to come from the east though he came from Chaldea. Keil and Delitzsch simply have them move from Ararat south-eastward into a broad plain, and note that the word is not a valley between mountains but the sort of level ground Herodotus calls a great plain about Babylon. Ellicott adds that the verb for journeying is the pulling up of tent-pegs, which sets the family before us as nomads shifting their camp as the cattle needed pasture, and that the soil they stopped on is alluvial and immensely rich, still growing at the head of the Persian Gulf.

The building materials are read as evidence of two things, the poverty of the site and the determination of the builders. Clarke and Wesley both note that the plain yielded neither stone nor lime, so brick had to serve for stone and bitumen for mortar. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the bricks were burnt through rather than merely dried in the sun as ordinary eastern building requires, so that they became stone, and that asphalt abounds in that neighbourhood and may still be seen in the ruins. Ellicott makes the same point a mark of progress, since these nomads had learned that clay burnt becomes insoluble, and adds a traveller's report from the ruins of Birs-Nimroud that the bricks could scarcely be detached from one another, so tenacious was the cement. Calvin turns the difficulty into an aggravation of the guilt. They were not drawn on by the ease of the work but contended with great and arduous difficulties, and he asks why men should wear themselves out on so laborious an enterprise unless, like madmen, they were rushing against God; difficulty deters us from necessary works, yet these men, having neither stone nor mortar, did not scruple to attempt a building that should transcend the clouds. He quotes a heathen poet to the same effect, that the human race rushes headlong through what is forbidden, and that nothing is too steep for mortals, who in their folly make for heaven itself. Wesley states plainly what the builders were after. Two things, he says: to make themselves a name, doing something posterity would talk of, and to prevent their dispersion. Neither succeeded. History has not preserved the name of so much as one of them, though one Jewish writer says each engraved his own upon a brick; and as for the second aim, God had ordered them to scatter and they answered that they would live and die together, resolving to make this city the metropolis of a single empire and the centre of their unity. He mentions and dismisses the old guess that the tower was meant as a refuge against another flood, since men with that in view would have built on a mountain rather than a plain.
4:
What the tower was for is the largest question in the chapter, and hardly two of them answer it alike. The oldest guess, that it was a refuge against a second flood, is rejected on every side. Gill says they had God's covenant and oath against another, and would in any case have built on a mountain rather than a plain lying between two great rivers, since brickwork could never stand such a force of water. Ellicott dismisses the same notion along with the stories of Nimrod's impiety and of a defiance of God, holding that there is not the least vestige of authority for any of it in the record. Clarke reports two other proposals instead. One makes the structure a temple to the host of heaven, its head being in the heavens taken to mean the heavenly bodies, and one lip taken to mean one litany, so that what God confounded was their worship and they broke thereafter into sects. The other is the claim of the Targums that the tower was for idolatry from the first, with an image to stand on the top holding a sword as a talisman against enemies. Clarke will not decide between them, but observes that whatever the original design, the building was afterwards given over to idolatry, repaired by Nebuchadnezzar and dedicated to Bel.

Ellicott offers the most worldly reading of the four. He finds a double object, first a central beacon to guide the wanderers home from their journeys, and then something more ambitious, since a people that stayed one nation could reduce to obedience all the tribes drifting away from it and so make itself a name. That, he says, is what is now called centralisation, by which the individual gives up his rights to the nation and the provinces to the capital, so that the force of the whole body can be brought to bear at once; he grants it many advantages and thinks some able and ambitious mind was probably behind the scheme — then adds, remembering the blood-stained course of some of Nimrod's cities, that he doubts whether centralisation really promotes human happiness. On the height he is deflating: the Hebrew is far less hyperbolical than our version, saying only that the top is in the heavens, exactly as the walls of the Canaanite cities are described.

Calvin will have nothing in it but the name. The phrase about the top is plainly hyperbolical, a boast about the loftiness of what they meant to raise, and the wish for a name means that the work should be talked of to the world's utmost limits. He calls this the perpetual infatuation of the world, to neglect heaven and seek immortality on earth where everything is fading, and sets a psalm and a satirist side by side on it: David holds the blind cupidity up to ridicule, and Juvenal says that death alone confesses how small the bodies of men are. Even death, Calvin adds, does not cure our pride, since more of it is often displayed at funerals than at weddings, and he draws from that the counsel to keep death before our eyes in the midst of life for the sake of moderation. On the last clause he refuses two readings and gives a third. It cannot mean before we are scattered, the language will not bear it; and the guesses that Noah had warned them, or that they prophesied their own punishment without understanding it, he calls constrained. What they knew was simply that the earth was made to be inhabited and that a people multiplying so fast could not stay long within narrow limits; so wherever they might have to go, they meant the tower to stand behind them as a witness of where they came from.
5:
The verse says God came down, and every voice here treats that as speech fitted to us rather than a report of divine movement. Gill denies it is local or visible. God is immense, omnipresent and invisible. Nor did he come down in order to learn what he could not see from heaven, for he is omniscient. The phrase covers some effect and display of his power that made his presence plain. Gill passes on the Targum, which renders it that the Lord was revealed to take vengeance on them for the business of the city and the tower. Calvin says the same in his own way: the descent is spoken with reference to men rather than to God, who does not move from place to place. What it marks is that God appeared gradually, and as with a tardy step, in the character of an Avenger. He descended that he might see, which is to say he showed plainly that he was not ignorant of what the Babylonians were attempting. Wesley states it most briefly. He knew it as clearly as men know a thing they have come to the place to view.

The greater interest for these writers is the pattern of judgment the phrase discloses. Gill finds in it both patience and justice. God did not proceed against the builders at once, and he took cognizance of the case, examining the truth of the matter before passing sentence. Henry puts it as a rule: before he gave judgment upon their cause he enquired into it, for God condemns none unheard. Clarke has only a line, quoting an ancient Jewish commentator that this is a lesson to magistrates to examine every evidence before they decree judgment. Henry adds that the coming down is itself condescension, since God humbles himself to behold the transactions of this lower world. Calvin explains the delay differently, and more severely. God for a little while seemed to take no notice, so that by breaking the work off suddenly at its commencement he might give the more decisive evidence of his judgment. He often bears with the wicked so far as to further their designs with animating success, that he may at length cast them down to a lower depth. Henry reaches a similar point by a gentler road. God let them proceed a good way to give them space to repent, and, failing that, so that their disappointment might be the more shameful: these men began to build, and were not able to finish.

The phrase children of men draws out three things for Henry, and Wesley abridges him on all three. It marks their frailty, for it was a foolish thing in worms of the earth to defy heaven; are they stronger than he? It marks their sin, since the Hebrew reads sons of Adam, of that disobedient Adam whose children are by nature children of disobedience. And it marks their separation from the children of God, from whom these builders had parted, raising the tower to perpetuate the breach; pious Eber is not found among them. Henry then gives the two considerations on which the sentence turned. Their oneness was itself a danger, for while they held together much of the earth would lie uninhabited, their prince would grow exorbitant, and they would strengthen one another's hands in wickedness. Their obstinacy was the other, for commands and admonitions had already failed. From the first Henry draws a rebuke rather than a comfort. Unity is a policy, but not the infallible mark of a true church, and it shames the builders of Zion that men of different families and interests were unanimous in opposing God while his own people are divided in serving him.
6:
The plural in let us go down is the first question here, and the answers agree. Gill denies the words are spoken to angels, against Aben Ezra and the Targum, and cites Philo: those addressed are treated as fellow workers. Angels cannot be that, since it is beyond any creature to work upon the mind and the faculty of speech as this judgment did, whether by putting a new tongue into them or by so altering the old one that it seemed several. Only the Almighty can do it, and so the words are the Father speaking to the Son and the Spirit. Wesley says it plainly: not to the angels, as if God needed their advice or their assistance. Calvin rejects the Jewish reading on a different ground. No angels are mentioned, and God places those he addresses in the same rank with himself, so the exposition is harsh and deservedly rejected. The passage answers instead to let us make man after our image, and Calvin thinks it not improperly adduced in proof that three Persons subsist in one essence of Deity. Clarke handles only the opening particle: go to now means nothing in English, while the Hebrew carries come, or make ready, as the Greek and Latin render it.

On the tone of the sixth verse Calvin canvasses two readings before giving his own. Some take it for complaint, God stirring himself by righteous grief, not that he is swayed by passions, but to teach that he is no more negligent of the wickedness of the ungodly than of the safety of his own. Others hear an argument from less to greater: what will they dare as many nations, if they dare this while few? Calvin finds rather a suppressed irony, as though God set himself a hard task. This people is welded into a firm conspiracy and speaks one language; by what method can they be broken? He smiles at their confidence, for men reckoning on their own strength arrogate everything to themselves. In the next verse Calvin says Moses paints the scene so that the judgment stands before the eye, and puts the sentence in God's own mouth: I will not use many instruments, I will only blow upon them. They had gathered a band to reach the clouds; God musters his forces against them, and Solomon's word holds, that there is no counsel nor prudence nor strength against the Lord. Wesley notes the fitness of the means. Men who cannot understand one another can neither help one another at the work nor enjoy one another in the place.

What the confusion was, Clarke tries to say. He supposes the first language monosyllabic, each word bearing one meaning, and thinks Chinese still such, and Hebrew nearly so if its points and affixes were separated. The judgment then was less the sudden coining of new tongues than a change in how the same word was sounded and understood, so that the hearer took the speaker in a contrary sense; he illustrates it from Du Bartas, where one man calls for a trowel and is brought a hammer. Clarke adds that the tongues of the earth were not formed in a moment, climate and trade and government all having their share, and observes that Arabic, Syriac and Ethiopic still bear a striking likeness to their parent. Wesley reckons the cost as continuing: we smart for Babel in every language we must learn, and perhaps in those controversies which are strifes of words. He judges the scheme of a universal character a vain thing, since it strives against a divine sentence. Both he and Calvin close where the wound is healed, at Pentecost, one gospel spoken in all tongues gathering what Babel scattered. Keil, treating these verses with the genealogy that follows, marks the paragraph as the close of the dispersion before the line returns to Shem.
8:
Gill states the irony that governs both verses. The very thing the builders feared came upon them, and it came by the measures they had taken to guard against it. Unable to understand one another they gave the work up, and those who shared a speech drew together and departed in bodies, until by degrees the whole earth was peopled, as God had willed. Ellicott describes the mechanism without any miracle beyond the first: as diversity of language grew, each tribe held intercourse only with those of its own dialect, so the divine purpose of occupying the world took effect while the project of this ambitious knot of men to hold mankind together was frustrated. Clarke presses the same point harder. God would not permit a single seat of government, and made the means devised to prevent dispersion the instrument of accomplishing it; humanly speaking the earth could not have been peopled so quickly otherwise. Calvin alone insists on a distinction. Men had already been spread abroad, and that was no punishment but flowed from blessing and grace; what happens here is different in kind. Those whom the Lord had before distributed with honour in various abodes he now ignominiously scatters, driving them hither and thither like the members of a lacerated body. This was not a simple dispersion for replenishing the earth, but a violent rout, because the principal bond of conjunction between them was cut asunder.

On the name Gill takes Babel for confusion, as the Greek renders it, and notes that Josephus says the Hebrews call confusion by this word. He guesses the sons of Eber may have fastened it on the place, and adds that though the first builders desisted, Nimrod afterwards carried the work on and made the city the beginning of his kingdom. Clarke derives it from a root meaning to mingle or confound, and repeats that the confusion lay less in the coining of new tongues than in a new pronouncing of the old words and a new sense fixed to them; the story of seventy-two nations with seventy-two languages he calls an idle and unfounded tale. Gill also reports heathen writers assigning the scattering to a divine hand, citing Eupolemus, whose flood survivors build Babylon and then the tower, which fell by the power of God and left the giants scattered. Calvin reads the name as the answer to the fourth verse. They had hoped an everlasting memorial of their origin would be engraven on the tower; God not only frustrates the expectation but brands them with lasting disgrace. They gain a name, but not such a one as they would have chosen.

Ellicott works the philology out at length. Babel is Bab-el, the gate of God, in Assyrian Bab-ili; he refuses the derivation from Bab-Bel, the gate of Bel, since there is no trace that the second letter was ever doubled and since Bel stands for Baal, whose guttural Orientals keep though Westerns drop it. Far from weakening the scriptural derivation, he thinks this strengthens it. Man calls his city the gate, that is the court, of God; God calls it Babble, for in every language confused speech is figured by the lips producing that sound, as the Hebrew balbal, the Greek bambaino, the Latin balbutio, and balbus for a stammerer. The town keeps its name with a contemptuous meaning fixed to it, much as Nabal did once his wife gave his name a turn. Ellicott adds that the Babylonian legends agree remarkably, making the building impious and a Titanic attempt on heaven, which he takes as evidence of its vast scale, since men attach impiety to stupendous undertakings and rejoice when they fail. Whether the tower was the temple of Bel in the city centre or the observatory at Borsippa two miles south, whose name Oppert reads as the tower of languages, he inclines to the latter.
10:
Gill states the limit of the list at once: it is not a genealogy of all Shem's posterity, but only of the line that led to Abraham, by which the true descent of the Messiah from Adam might appear. Henry makes the same point his opening. This is not an endless genealogy, for it ends in Abram the friend of God, and carries on to Christ the promised seed; set the fifth chapter, this one and the first of Matthew together, and you have a pedigree such as cannot be produced for any other person at such a distance from the fountain head. Twice ten and thrice fourteen descents, he counts, lie between the first Adam and the second, which establishes that Christ was son of Abraham, son of man, and seed of the woman. Clarke calls the line simply the holy family, since from it came Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the twelve patriarchs, David and Solomon. Calvin looks instead at what the chapter adds to the tenth, namely the term of each man's life; without this brief record we should not know how much time lay between the deluge and the covenant with Abram. He reads the choice of this family for the world's calendar as a mark of honour, as historians date their annals by kings or consuls.

What the passage withholds interests Henry more than what it gives, and Wesley follows him closely here. Nothing is left on record but names and ages, the Holy Ghost seeming to hasten through them to the story of Abram. How little we know of those gone before us, Henry says, even of those who lived where we live, and as little of our contemporaries in distant places; we have enough to do to mind our own day's work. The one thing the numbers do show is a steady decline. Shem reached six hundred years, already short of the patriarchs before the flood; the next three fell short of five hundred, the next three did not reach three hundred, and after them none but Terah attained two hundred, until Moses reckoned seventy or eighty the utmost. Henry will not put this down to any decay of nature. As the earth began to be replenished men's lives began to shorten, and the change is to be imputed to the wise disposal of Providence. He notes one exception with approval. Eber, from whom the Hebrews were named, outlived all who were born after the flood, which was perhaps the reward of his strict adherence to the ways of God.

The numbers themselves are contested, and Clarke says so plainly. Scripture chronology as it stands in the Hebrew, the Samaritan, the Greek, Josephus and some of the fathers is greatly embarrassed, and worse in the chronologists' systems; he sends his reader to Hales rather than argue it out. One instance he does settle: the Greek inserts a second Cainan with an added hundred and thirty years, and Luke follows the Greek, but the Hebrew both here and in Chronicles is silent, and the best chronologists reject the generation as spurious. The closing verse raises a second difficulty, and Gill and Clarke resolve it the same way. Abram is named first but was not the eldest; Haran was, and Abram was born in his father's hundred and thirtieth year, since Terah died at two hundred and five and Abram left Haran at seventy-five. Clarke adds that Scripture sets the youngest first where dignity is in view, as Shem before his brothers and Moses before Aaron. Gill fills the interval with darker notices: idolatry spread in Reu's days, and Terah was the first of this line to fall from the true religion. Calvin presses that hardest. From Shem's many sons God took Arphaxad alone, and from his sons Selah, and then Eber, and so to Abram, whose calling should be reckoned the renovation of the Church.
27:
Ellicott sets the heading in its place first. This tôldôth runs on to the eleventh verse of the twenty-fifth chapter, and he calls it one of the most interesting in Genesis, since it carries the history of Abraham, in whom God laid the foundation of the intermediate dispensation and of the Jewish Church, whose psalmists and prophets kept the light of true religion and made ready the way for Christ. Yet the section is headed with Terah's name, not Abraham's, as the history of Joseph is headed with Jacob's. Ellicott denies this is because Lot and his descendants figure in it, which he thinks subsidiary; the title joins Abraham to the past and shows him, through Terah and the line closing in him, the representative of Shem. Gill only notes how short the genealogy is, giving the three sons over again and no more. Henry opens the story rather than the section, and dwells on the country: Ur of the Chaldees, the land of Abram's nativity and an idolatrous land, where even the children of Eber had degenerated. Those who are by grace heirs of the promise, he says, ought to remember the land of their nativity, and the rock out of which they were hewn.

The verse names Abram first, and whether that makes him the eldest is the question the writers fight over. Henry states the case from the numbers. The twenty-sixth verse looks as though Abram were born in Terah's seventieth year, but Terah died at two hundred and five, and Abram left Haran at seventy-five after his father's death, so he was born in Terah's hundred and thirtieth year and was probably the youngest son; in God's choices, Henry adds, the last are often first and the first last. Wesley reproduces the reasoning. Calvin reaches the same conclusion and defends it at length. If Abram were born in the seventieth year we must lose sixty years of Terah's life, which is absurd; Luther's guess that God buried the time in oblivion to hide from us the end of the world he calls frivolous, and the suggestion that Abram lived sixty years with his father at Charran he thinks most improbable, for to what end should they protract their stay in the middle of the journey? Moses simply does not say in what year Terah begat his sons. Ellicott stands alone against all this. Commentators who deny Abram the birthright and give him first place for spiritual pre-eminence argue, he says, against the rules of the Hebrew language, and the failed attempt to strip Shem of his birthright by mistranslating an earlier verse only confirms Abram's claim to the same prerogative.

The relations are named, Henry says, for Abram's sake and because they figure in what follows. Of Terah it is said elsewhere that he served other gods beyond the river, so early did idolatry gain footing in the world, and so hard is it even for men of some good principle to swim against the stream. Nahor matters because both Isaac and Jacob took wives out of his family, and Haran because he was the father of Lot. Sarai some think the same with Iscah, Haran's daughter, though Abram himself says she was his father's daughter and not his mother's; she was ten years younger than he. Then the departure, in obedience to a call not yet recorded, with Terah, Lot and the rest of the household. Henry observes that the chapter leaves them at Charran, about midway between Ur and Canaan, where they stayed until Terah's head was laid, probably because the old man's infirmities would not let him go further. On that halt he hangs the warning the passage has left to readers ever since. Many reach to Charran and yet fall short of Canaan; they are not far from the kingdom of God, and yet never come thither.
28:
Haran's dying before his father is read by all three as a matter of presence rather than dates. Gill takes it for in his father's sight, with Jarchi and Aben Ezra, and says it marks the place more than the time, Terah being there. Ellicott renders it in the presence of his father, and calls this the first recorded premature death by natural decay. Calvin says only that Haran left his father the survivor, and that he died in his own country, in Ur. It is on the name of that country that Calvin spends his indignation. The Jews turn the proper name into a common noun, since Ur can be derived from fire, and forge the tale that Haran and Abram were thrown into a furnace for refusing idolatry, Abram escaping by the constancy of his faith. Joshua's charge that this whole family served other gods beyond the river is enough, Calvin thinks, to dispose of it, for the household was no less infected than the land. He grants the derivation from fire while denying the inference. Cities take their names from their situation or from some event; it may be that a sacred fire was kept there, or that the sun was seen more brightly than elsewhere. He will not be anxious about it.

Ellicott brings the cuneiform inscriptions to bear and gives the fullest account of the place. Ur of the Chaldees he identifies with the mounds of Mugheir. It was first held by Accadians, a Turanian people probably sprung from an offshoot of Japheth, and afterwards taken by Semites, who overran Shinar and drove out the descendants of Cush. He follows Sayce in placing the consolidation of the petty Chaldean kingdoms under Lig-Bagas about three thousand years before Christ, and notes that bricks and cylinders from that king's library lie in our museums, with an older Accadian literature behind them. The consequence he draws is the interesting one. Abraham left a famous seat of learning, where even ordinary transactions were kept on terra-cotta, and may well have carried such records with him; the resemblance between the earlier chapters of Genesis and the cuneiform narratives should no longer surprise us. Ellicott presses the unlikeness just as hard. The inscriptions own twelve superior gods and a countless multitude of inferior ones, and the Semites added goddesses to them, while of all this the biblical record keeps no trace, and Chaldean literature has nothing so grand as the opening words of Genesis. He adds that Ur was a walled town and the great port of the Persian Gulf.

The marriages of the two surviving brothers raise a small question of identity. Gill supposes they married after their elder brother's death, taking his daughters, and thinks perhaps both did. Clarke rejects the common view that Sarai and Iscah are one person under two names, since Iscah is expressly called Haran's daughter while Sarai was Terah's, and so Abram's half-sister. Ellicott agrees, and disposes of Ewald's guess that Iscah was Lot's wife, she being his full sister. Marriage between near relatives, he notes, was allowed then and perhaps common for religious reasons, but not between children of the same mother; so Abraham takes his half-sister and Nahor his niece. On Sarai's barrenness Gill records that Aben Ezra had heard the defect laid to Abram, which he calls the reverse of Scripture and refutes from Ishmael and the sons of Keturah. Calvin asks why the reason for the childlessness is given at all, and answers that it shows nothing short of a miracle brought Isaac. God meant to humble his servant, and the pain was severe: Abram watched the wicked multiply and cover the earth while he alone was left without children. In him, Calvin says, God was showing as in a mirror how his Church would arise, for it lay hid at that time like a dry root under the earth.
31:
Calvin thinks the next chapter ought to begin here, since Moses turns to one of the principal subjects of his book, the calling of Abram. What decides it is that Moses gives not only the change of country but its end, that they set out to come to Canaan. From that he infers that Terah was not so much the leader of the journey as the companion of his son. Moses names the father first, but that is an honour paid to him, and Calvin does not doubt that Abram, seeing his father obey the call of God, grew the more obedient in return. Abram had been called before he moved a foot from his native soil; of Terah no call is recorded, so the oracle likely reached him by his son's report. Gill lingers over the careful naming of Lot and Sarai and finds it leaves us in the dark. Aben Ezra puts the difficulty: had Sarai been Terah's daughter, the verse would have named her his daughter; had she been Lot's sister, it would have called her the daughter of his son, as it does Lot. Ellicott notes that the phrase they went forth with them is strange, and that a slight transposition of letters gives the Samaritan, Greek and Latin reading: Terah brought them forth.

Clarke takes up the country they left. Chaldea sometimes means all Babylonia and sometimes the province toward the desert; Ur was a city of consequence, though its site is not well known, and it probably drew its name from fire, the learned being nearly unanimous that its early inhabitants were fire-worshippers. He adds that the Chaldees bore that name not in the age Moses describes but in the age when he wrote, tracing them from Chesed, Nahor's son, and notes that those in Ur were priests or astronomers as well as idolaters; being so given to astrology, they lent their name to astrologers ever after. Ellicott identifies the halting-place: the Charran of Acts, Carrhae in north-west Mesopotamia, some twenty miles south-east of Edessa, not to be confounded with Haran the father of Lot, since the Hebrew spells it otherwise. In Accadian the word means road, and Sayce calls the town the key of the highway east to west. On the motive Ellicott offers two. Partly the move was a northward drift of Semites made restless by the Elamites then overrunning Western Asia; but chiefly it was religious, Ur being the especial seat of the moon-god, and Terah, though short of the purity of Abraham's faith, no mere idolater either.

Why the family stopped short of Canaan Calvin answers from the arithmetic. Terah must have left his country only a little before his death, for it is absurd that a man bound directly for Canaan should stay sixty years on the road; more likely an old man worn with years was carried off by disease and weariness. God may have held them briefly in suspense, since Moses says he dwelt in Charran, but the delay cannot have been long, Abram leaving in his seventy-fifth year. Gill observes that Terah's years are summed up as no one else's are here, so the reader might mark them, his death being the moment Abram left Chaldea; he reports an Arabic historian giving Terah two hundred and sixty-five years, sixty too many, and guesses Terah named the place after his dead son. Ellicott adds that by the Samaritan text Abram left in the year his father died, and that Nahor had probably joined the household by then, being later found settled there. Clarke closes by counting the chapter's three great particulars, the building of Babel, the confusion of tongues and the call of Abram, and the three ends they served: the peopling of the earth, the keeping of true religion in one family, and the preserving of the line by which the Messiah should come.
